entities.name: John XVI
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John XVI, originally named John Philagathos, was a Byzantine Greek cleric who served as antipope from 997 to 998, challenging the authority of Pope Gregory V and Emperor Otto III. Born in Rossano, Calabria (then part of the Byzantine Catapanate of Italy), he rose through the ecclesiastical ranks due to his connections with the imperial court, serving as a chaplain to Empress Theophanu and later as the abbot of Nonantola. His elevation to the papacy by the powerful Roman patrician Crescentius II represented a direct confrontation with the Ottonian imperial power, seeking to reassert local Roman control over the Holy See in the turbulent late 10th century.

Philagathos's path to the antipapacy began with his appointment as Bishop of Piacenza and his role as an imperial envoy to Constantinople. After the death of Emperor Otto II, Crescentius II seized the opportunity provided by young Otto III's minority and Gregory V's initial unpopularity in Rome to install John XVI. In 997, with Byzantine support, he was consecrated antipope, forcing Gregory V to flee to Pavia. However, Otto III, upon reaching maturity, swiftly marched on Rome in 998. John XVI attempted to escape but was captured, subjected to brutal mutilation—his eyes, nose, and tongue were removed, and his fingers were severed—before being publicly paraded through Rome. He was then formally deposed and imprisoned in the monastery of Fulda, where he died around 1001.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John XVI's brief anti-papacy and subsequent brutal deposition underscored the ongoing struggle between imperial and local Roman power for control of the papacy, setting a harsh precedent for dealing with rival claimants. His story illustrates the volatile political landscape of 10th-century Italy and the strength of Ottonian imperial authority.
